description:
In 1914, a ship sailing from New York to San Francisco no longer had to round Cape Horn. A voyage of about 13,000 miles shrank to roughly 5,200, thanks to a channel about 51 miles long cut across the Isthmus of Panama. This documentary tells how it was built, and what it cost.

We follow the French attempt under Ferdinand de Lesseps, the builder of the Suez Canal, which began in 1881 and collapsed in 1889 after yellow fever, malaria and landslides took an estimated 22,000 lives. We see how Panama broke away from Colombia in November 1903, how the United States took over the works in 1904, and how Dr. William Gorgas defeated the mosquito. Then chief engineers John Stevens and George Goethals drove the Culebra Cut through the Continental Divide, raised the Gatun Dam to create what was then the largest artificial lake in the world, and built locks 110 feet wide and 1,000 feet long.

The SS Ancon made the first official transit on August 15, 1914. The American effort cost about 375 million dollars and roughly 5,600 lives, much of the hardest labor done by workers from the Caribbean. In 1999 the canal passed to Panama, and in 2016 a new set of larger locks opened.

Sources include Wikipedia articles on the Panama Canal and its history. Figures for distances and deaths are commonly cited estimates.
